subject: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models

messages.author: 8f67c813ac59bbcb
messages.subject: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models
parts:
Hello everyone!

I’m currently working on a single-species occupancy model using survey data collected from 2019 to 2023. I would like to include a dynamic vegetation variable that changes daily. My initial approach was to include it as a detection covariate, but I keep running into formatting errors when trying to do so.

I’m starting to wonder if this is the right approach. Do you have any suggestions on how best to include a daily-changing covariate in the model?

Thank you for your help!

Best regards,

Arianna Vicari

messages.author: f65cdebf441dbb1a
messages.subject: Re: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models
parts:
Dear Arianna,

that sounds like a sensible idea, if you think that vegetation height might affect detection probability. However, when you say daily values for the covariate, then that requires that you also organize your detection/nondetection data by daily occasions --- is this so ? If not (e.g., if you have weekly occasions), then you will have to summarize the covariate by occasion as well.

Can you be more explicit what kinds of errors you encounter ?

Best regards  ---- Marc

messages.subject: Re: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models
parts:
Hi Marc,

Thank you for the explanation.
My data (from camera traps) is structured with daily records for 91 cameras across 2610 days. The detection covariates I currently include are:

  • Effort (number of days each camera was deployed), and

  • Dynamic MSAVI, with one value per camera per day when the camera was active (NA when the camera was not active).

I think I have now fixed the formatting issue I mentioned before, but I would appreciate your opinion on whether structuring the data in this way (daily resolution for both detections and MSAVI) is appropriate.

In addition, I am wondering how inference rasters should be handled in this case. If MSAVI is included as a daily covariate, does this imply that I would need to generate a prediction raster for each day, or is there a more standard approach to representing such dynamic covariates in the inference stage?

I thank you in advance for the help.

Kindly,

Arianna Vicari

messages.author: f65cdebf441dbb1a
messages.subject: Re: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models
parts:
Dear Arianna,

thanks for this information. Purely format-wise, this looks OK. But, to be honest, I have some big questions about your analysis. First of all, I have never seen an occupancy model that was fit to data that span 7 years. Clearly, you can't assume closure over such a long period (unless perhaps your study system is some big tree); I'd bet a lot of money that your population is open over this duration. Hence, you must address this in some way. (Apologies if you intend to adopt a model that accommodates an open population, but this is not apparent from your email.)

Then, daily temporal resolution is almost certainly overkill. At least, if your main questions are about occupancy, I'd perhaps envision weekly or monthly occasions. (If you want to model detection probability as a way of inferring something about the behaviour of the animals, then perhaps this resolution might be OK.)

Your decisions about how to discretize time into primary occasions (e.g., years, springs or mating seasons) and into secondary ones (e.g., weeks or months, as just mentioned) will depend on the dynamics of your study system and importantly also on your questions. So, what questions do you want to answer with your occupancy model ?

Best regards  ---- Marc

messages.author: 8f67c813ac59bbcb
messages.subject: Re: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models
parts:
Dear Marc, dear Jeff,

Thank you very much for your useful insights about the model.

I am answering just now, as I tried a couple things to work out the problem I had at the beginning.

To answer your questions:

  • The target species population is very limited in both size and spatial occurrence, so we are comfortable treating it as a closed population.

  • The other species considered (both wild and domestic) are more likely to have open populations.

Our overall goals are to:

  1. Understand which factors influence the spatial distribution of animals (e.g., terrain, food resources, livestock, or human presence).

  2. Compare the three wild species in terms of distributions, influential factors, and what makes one of them more vulnerable than the others.

To mitigate the issue with the large dataset, I divided it into two study periods (2017–2020 and 2022–2024), given the assumption of population closure described above. 

I also included several covariates in both the occurrence and detectability formulas. So far, for the spatial single-species models of two (out of the three) species, everything seems to be running smoothly.

The problem lies with one species: no matter how many variables I include in the model or how I relax certain priors, I cannot obtain a Bayesian p-value higher than 0.1 (they remain around 0.003). I suspect I might be overlooking something, as I cannot explain this result, especially since the other species living in the same environment fit the models properly when I adjust the variables.

Could this be due to limited detection/non-detection data, restricted spatial variance, or the influence of specific priors? Or do you think it might reflect something truly species-specific (such as behavioral or spatial preferences) that my current covariates fail to capture?

Thank you again for your valuable guidance.

Kindly,

Arianna Vicari

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: Question about Including Daily Vegetation in Occupancy Models
parts:
Hi Arianna,

Apologies for the delay in response. If you're fitting a spatial occupancy model for that species and exploring a variety of different models with different covariates, my guess is that the low Bayesian p-value is a result of additional variation in detection probability in the species that you are not accounting for, either spatially and/or temporally within replicates. If the species is extremely rare, then it may be difficult to get a good fit on the species as indicated by the Bayesian p-value. I would encourage you to explore the output from the Bayesian p-value more in depth as opposed to only looking at the summary value, which can help indicate where any lack of fit may be arising from. For example, see some of the graphs made in the introductory vignette. If the problem is extra variation in detection probability that cannot be explained by the covariates in your model, then you may explore the use of random effects in your detection model formula. For example, site-level random effects in detection could help account for extra spatial variation in detection probability you aren't accounting for, but these can also be difficult to estimate for a species without a lot of detections.

Kind regards,

Jeff
